785.title: Sadhna's plea for grace
785.hook: Sadhna, remembered as a butcher, pleads to be saved by grace (Bilaval, Sadhna, ang 858)
785.howItsDone: Sadhna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the Lord's gracious glance, as a gift that can be asked for but never earned or forced.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaaiaa: deity, temple and pilgrim, all found in the body. Today, a devotee argues with God for grace.

A lifeguard waits until the swimmer has gone under for good, then rows out with a boat. What use is that? Sadhna asks almost exactly that question, out loud, to God. Tradition remembers him as a butcher, and his hymn sits in the Guru Granth Sahib all the same. It isn't calm. It's urgent, a little bold, and full of arguments. He isn't asking whether grace exists. He's asking for it now.
screen: `A BOAT AFTER THE SWIMMER DROWNS.` → `REMEMBERED AS A BUTCHER.` → `GRACE, AND NOW.`

segments.voice: Sadhna's hymn is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang 858, and he argues like someone who knows he can't earn what he's asking for. First, in paraphrase: O Guru of the world, what good are Your virtues if my karma isn't wiped away? Why run to a lion for shelter, if a jackal is going to eat you anyway? The point of refuge is that it's stronger than what's chasing you. Second, the chaatrik, the rainbird of Indian poetry that longs for a single raindrop. For one drop, the bird suffers; once its life is gone, an ocean is no use to it. Third, the boat. My life is worn out and unsteady, he says; how can I wait? If I drown and die, and then a boat arrives, tell me, who will you put on board? Each picture says the same thing from a new side: grace that comes too late isn't grace. Then everything drops away. In paraphrase: I am nothing, I have nothing, nothing at all is mine. At this moment, protect my honor; Sadhna is Your servant. That's the plea. Not a list of good deeds, because he doesn't claim any. Just empty hands and a deadline. Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy. Sadhna's hymn is what asking for that glance sounds like when there's nothing left to bargain with.
screen: `THE LION AND THE JACKAL.` · `ONE DROP FOR THE RAINBIRD.` · `A BOAT AFTER DROWNING IS NO USE.` · then, large: `I HAVE NOTHING; SAVE ME NOW.`

segments.voice: Find the place where effort has run out: a habit you can't break, a relationship you can't fix, a fear you can't argue away. Don't make a case for yourself; if you pray, ask once, simply, for grace there, and if you don't, just name it honestly, once, with empty hands like Sadhna's. Then breathe, with Waheguru on each breath out if you like.
Nadar. The gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy: Sadhna's plea when there was nothing left to bargain with.
Your line: saved by grace. A boat after the drowning is no use, so Sadhna asks now. Seven hundred eighty-five days, and counting.

786.title: Ramanand: where shall I go
786.hook: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love (Basant, Ramanand, ang 1195)
786.howItsDone: Ramanand's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Basant, and Sikh teaching speaks of finding the Lord within, guided by the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar: the lion and the jackal, the rainbird, the boat that comes too late, and a plea for grace. Today, a trip that never happens.

The bag is packed. The offering is ready: sandalwood, ground fine, mixed with sweet oils, the good stuff saved for a holy day. You're at the door, keys in hand, about to set out for the temple. And then you stop, set the bag down, and don't go. Not out of laziness. Because something just became clear. That's where Ramanand's hymn begins: at the door.
screen: `SANDALWOOD READY, BAG PACKED.` → `AT THE DOOR, YOU STOP.` → `RAMANAND'S HYMN BEGINS THERE.`

segments.voice: Three days ago, Sain the barber named a teacher: Ramanand, who knows the devotion of the Lord. Today Ramanand speaks for himself, in Raag Basant, the raag of spring, on Ang 1195. It opens with a question, in paraphrase: where shall I go? My own home is colored with love. My mind no longer wanders off; it has gone still. Then he tells how. One day a longing rose up in me. I ground sandalwood with fragrant oils and set out to worship God at the holy place. And the Guru showed me that God within my own mind. The trip turned around at the door. Next, a line with a gentle sting. Wherever I go, I find water and stone: bathing places and carved images. But You fill them all, equally. I've looked through the Vedas and the Puranas, the old scriptures. Go there, he says, only if He isn't here. He doesn't say the temple is empty or the old books worthless. He says the One who fills the temple fills the home too, and everything equally, so the long walk isn't needed to find what's already here. The close, in paraphrase: True Guru, I'm a sacrifice to You, who cut away all my confusion and doubt. Ramanand's Lord is the all-pervading One, and the Guru's Word cuts away countless deeds. Tradition remembers Ramanand as a teacher whose circle reached far, and some say Kabir learned from him. In the Granth, he leaves one image: a house dyed with love, so full there's nowhere else to go.

segments.voice: Stay right where you are, in whatever room this is, and don't wish yourself somewhere holier: notice the wall, the light, the sounds from the next room or the street. If the mind wants to pack a bag and go somewhere better, let it set the bag down. If you pray, say Waheguru on the breath out; if you don't, simply stay.
Ramanand. The teacher Sain named, whose hymn in Raag Basant turns around at the door: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love?
Your line: colored at home. The room you're in counts, just as it is. Until tomorrow.

787.title: Parmanand: hear, then do
787.hook: what use is hearing holy stories if devotion doesn't follow (Sarang, Parmanand, ang 1253)
787.howItsDone: Parmanand's hymn in Raag Sarang is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs read it as a call to let what is heard in the gurdwara change how they live and give.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramanand: where shall I go, when my own home is colored with love? Today, a hard question about listening.

A cookbook on the nightstand, its pages soft from reading in bed. Every recipe known by heart. The oven has never been switched on. Reading about bread is a real pleasure. It just doesn't feed anybody. In Raag Sarang, on Ang 1253 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Parmanand turns to someone who has heard every holy story there is, and asks a blunt question: so what did all that listening do?
screen: `A COOKBOOK READ IN BED.` → `THE OVEN NEVER ON.` → `WHAT DID THE LISTENING DO?`

segments.voice: Parmanand is one of the Bhagats, the devotees outside the line of the Gurus whose words sit in the Granth. The Granth tells almost nothing about his life; what it keeps is his hymn. It opens, in paraphrase: man, what have you gained by hearing the Puranas? Steady devotion never rose up in you, and you gave nothing to the hungry. The Puranas are old books of sacred stories, gods and kings and devotees, read aloud and loved. Parmanand isn't sneering at the stories. He's looking at the listener who walks away from them unchanged. Then he names what didn't move: lust and anger and greed are still there, and the mouth still hasn't stopped speaking ill of others. The stories went in at the ears and stopped. Look at his test. Not how many stories you know, or how beautifully you retell them. Two plain questions: did devotion grow, and did the hungry get fed? A heart turned toward God, and a hand turned toward the person in front of you, named side by side, and the listener has neither. The Granth keeps that question in his own voice. Which is a little awkward for a lesson like this one, since a lesson is also something heard. A story heard is a seed in a pocket. Parmanand's question is whether it ever goes into the ground.
screen: `WHAT DID HEARING THE PURANAS GAIN YOU?` · `NOT THE STORIES: THE UNCHANGED LISTENER.` · `TWO TESTS: DEVOTION, AND THE HUNGRY FED.` · `A SEED IN A POCKET.` · then, large: `HEAR, THEN DO.`

segments.voice: Bring back one story from this path lately: Sain offering his work, Pipa finding the temple in the body, Ramanand at home in a house colored with love. Hold it, and ask what it would look like as one small thing done, a meal shared, a sharp word left unsaid, until it feels like a plan instead of a wish. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.
Parmanand. A Bhagat whose hymn in Raag Sarang asks what the hearing was for, if devotion never grew and the hungry went unfed.
Your line: hear, then do. Listening is the start, not the finish. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

788.title: Surdas's single line
788.hook: a single line: leave the company of those turned away from the Lord (Sarang, Surdas, ang 1253)
788.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of sangat, the company of those who remember God, as something that shapes a person, and gather in the gurdwara partly to keep that company; Surdas's line is read in that light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Parmanand asked what all the listening was for: hear, then do. Today, a teaching so short it's one line.

Some parts of the Guru Granth Sahib run on for pages: long ballads, rows and rows of saloks. Then, in Raag Sarang, on the same Ang as yesterday's hymn, there's the name Surdas, and with it a single line. No verses after it, no story around it. It sits there like a note pinned to a door on the way out. Somebody decided one line was worth keeping, and it carries Surdas's name.
screen: `PAGES OF BALLADS AND SALOKS.` → `A HEADING: SURDAS.` → `ONE LINE, PINNED TO THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase: O mind, leave the company of those who have turned away from the Lord. The key word is bemukh: one whose face is turned the other way. Not a cartoon villain. Someone whose whole attention points away from God. Who was this Surdas? Tradition tells more than one story about the name, and the Granth doesn't settle it. What it gives is the line, and where it puts it. Just before it stands a hymn headed with Guru Arjan's mark and the name Surdas together, about the Lord's people who live close to the Lord. So one page holds both sides of the same idea: the company that draws you near, and the company that turns you away. Now the hard part, because a line like this can be misused. It isn't a license to look down on anyone. Sikh teaching puts great weight on sangat, the company you keep, because company shapes a mind the way water shapes a stone, slowly and without asking. The line talks to the mind, not to the neighbors. It doesn't say: judge them. It says: notice what you're sitting in. People, voices, feeds and habits: some turn the face toward what matters, and some turn it away a little more each day, so slowly it's easy to miss. Surdas doesn't argue the case. One line, and the choosing is left to you.
screen: `O MIND, LEAVE THE COMPANY OF THE TURNED-AWAY.` · `BEMUKH: THE FACE TURNED THE OTHER WAY.` · `TWO SIDES ON ONE PAGE.` · `SANGAT SHAPES A MIND, NOT A LICENSE TO JUDGE.` · then, large: `ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Let the last few days pass in front of you: the people, the voices in your ears, the screens, the conversations. Without judging anyone, notice which left your face turned toward what you care about, and which turned it away. If you pray, breathe out Waheguru and rest in the good company you found.
Bemukh. One whose face is turned away from the Lord: Surdas's single line, kept whole, telling the mind to leave that company.
Your line: one line. Some teachings fit on a note pinned to a door. That's day seven hundred eighty-eight.

789.title: Jaidev, the old poet
789.hook: the poet of the Gita Govinda has two hymns in the Granth (Gujri, Jaidev, ang 526)
789.howItsDone: Jaidev's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Gujri and Raag Maru like other Gurbani, and Sikh readers hear in them the remembrance of the one Lord and the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bemukh: O mind, leave the company of those turned away. Today, a famous love poet turns up in the Granth.

The Gita Govinda is a love poem in Sanskrit about Krishna and Radha: longing, quarrels, reunion in the forest by the river. Its poet is Jaidev. Now open the Guru Granth Sahib to Raag Gujri, Ang 526, and there's that same name at the head of a hymn. It isn't the only one: Jaidev has two hymns in the Granth. The singer of the forest romance, on the same pages as the Gurus.
screen: `A LOVE POEM: KRISHNA AND RADHA.` → `THE SAME NAME IN RAAG GUJRI.` → `TWO HYMNS IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Start with how the Gujri hymn sounds. Its language leans hard on Sanskrit, the old learned tongue, so when it's sung it has a different ring from the Punjabi and Hindi around it. Same book, older accent. Now what it says. In paraphrase: the Lord was there before everything, beyond compare, true, lovely beyond telling, beyond nature itself. Then the turn: chant only the Name of the Lord, sweet, the very essence of nectar. Remember Him, and the fear of birth, old age and death no longer has a hold. Then he gets practical. He asks for purity in three places at once: in what you do, what you say, and what you think. Not one of the three. All of them, lined up. Set that beside his fame. The poet of a lush romance of gods in a forest is kept in the Granth for something spare: one Lord, beyond compare, and the Name. The hymn even asks, in paraphrase, what yoga, sacrifice, charity or austerity are worth beside that devotion. Some readers hear the Gurus keeping the part of an old poet's voice that rings with their own. Others say simply that the Granth honors devotion wherever it was sung. Either way, an old name sits on the page, sung in the same kirtan as everything else, asking for one life lined up three ways.
screen: `AN OLDER ACCENT: SANSKRIT IN THE SOUND.` · `BEFORE EVERYTHING, BEYOND COMPARE.` · `THE NAME, AND NO FEAR OF DEATH.` · `PURE IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT.` · then, large: `THE OLD POET.`

segments.voice: Take Jaidev's three places, one per breath. On the first, look at something you did today; on the next, something you said; on the next, something you thought, gently, and keep the cycle going. If you pray, let Waheguru close each round.
Jaidev. The poet of the Gita Govinda, whose hymns in the Granth praise the one Lord beyond compare and the sweet Name.
Your line: the old poet. Deed, word and thought, pointing the same way. See you tomorrow.

790.title: Bhikhan's medicine
790.hook: Bhikhan calls the Name the medicine for every illness (Sorath, Bhikhan, ang 659)
790.howItsDone: Bhikhan's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Sorath, and Sikh teaching speaks of naam, remembering God's Name, as healing for the mind, alongside ordinary care for the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaidev, the old poet: one Lord beyond compare, and purity in deed, word and thought. Today, an old man asks for a doctor.

The bathroom cabinet. Something for a headache, something for a cough, a half-used tube for a burn, a bottle with a date long gone. Every shelf has a cure for one particular thing. Bhagat Bhikhan, in Raag Sorath on Ang 659, writes from the other side of all those shelves: an old body, eyes running, voice failing. And he names a single medicine, for every illness.
screen: `A CABINET OF CURES.` → `ONE FOR EACH THING.` → `ONE MEDICINE FOR EVERY ILLNESS.`

segments.voice: He starts with the body, and doesn't flatter it. In paraphrase: water streams from the eyes, the body has grown thin, the hair has turned white as milk. The throat is choked, and the words won't come. Then the question to himself: what can you do now? It's an honest picture of old age, the kind that's easy to look away from. Then the doctor appears. In paraphrase: O Lord, my King, be the physician, and save your devotees. He doesn't ask God to stop him aging. He asks for a healer of a different kind. Then the hymn goes under the skin: the head aches, the body burns, the heart is in pain, a pain no medicine reaches. And he names one. The Name of the Lord is pure nectar water, the finest medicine in all the world. In the hymn that follows, he calls that Name a jewel beyond price. A medicine is taken regularly, not once. It works from the inside. It doesn't ask whether you deserve it. That's how Bhikhan speaks of the Name: remembered again and again, working where no ointment reaches. And to be clear about what he isn't saying: the hymn doesn't tell anyone to throw out the cabinet, or to skip the doctor. Read this way, Bhikhan is talking about the ache underneath the aches: fear, restlessness, the sense of being far from God. For that, he names one medicine: the Name of the Lord.
screen: `EYES RUNNING, HAIR WHITE AS MILK.` · `LORD, BE THE PHYSICIAN.` · `THE NAME: JEWEL, NECTAR, MEDICINE.` · `NOT INSTEAD OF A DOCTOR: UNDER THE ACHES.` · then, large: `THE NAME AS MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Find the ache that isn't in a muscle: a worry, a restless loop, a heaviness. Don't fix it; let the breath come and go across it slowly, the way you'd let a medicine work. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, a dose taken again and again; if you don't, let the quiet itself be the dose.
Bhikhan's medicine. In Raag Sorath, an old devotee asks the Lord to be his physician, and calls the Name the medicine for every illness.
Your line: the name as medicine. Not instead of the doctor, but for the ache underneath. Seven hundred ninety days now.

791.title: The Bhatts
791.hook: court poets whose swayyas praise the Gurus as one light (Swayye, ang 1389–1409)
791.howItsDone: The Bhatts' swayye are read and sung in the Guru Granth Sahib like the rest of Gurbani, and Sikhs turn to them for the teaching that the light of Guru Nanak passed whole from Guru to Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhikhan asked the Lord to be his physician, and named the Name as medicine. Today, poets who praised for a living.

A wedding toast. Somebody stands, clinks a glass, and praises the couple. Good toasts are a craft: specific, warm, a little grand. Now take people whose whole trade was that craft, praising the great for a living, and send them into the court of the Gurus. That's who the Bhatts were, as tradition tells it: bards, poets of praise. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang 1389, their verses fill page after page.
screen: `A TOAST IS A CRAFT.` → `BARDS WHO PRAISED FOR A LIVING.` → `THEIR VERSES NEAR THE END OF THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Their verses are called swayye, after the swayya, a form of poem, and they're grouped by Guru: for the first Guru, the second, and on through the fifth. So the Bhatts aren't Bhagats from distant centuries. Tradition places them in the time of Guru Arjan, looking at the line of Gurus and singing what they saw. And what they saw was one light. One poet, Bhatt Mathura, lays it out in a single verse, in paraphrase: the Lord, in the form of light, was called Guru Nanak; from him came Angad, essence merged with essence; Angad set Amar Das firm; Amar Das gave Ram Das the royal canopy; now see Guru Arjan, the fifth. Like a lamp lit from a lamp. Different bodies, the same light. Praise poetry can stop at the person: this king's sword, that king's wealth. The Bhatts do praise the Gurus warmly, their wisdom, their steadiness, their nearness to God. But underneath is a claim about what passes between them. Sikh readers hear these verses as a witness, from outside the family, to the teaching that the Guru is one, whatever body the light is in. They also close a week of the Granth's other voices: Sadhna pleading for grace, Ramanand at home in a house colored with love, Parmanand asking what the hearing was for, Surdas and his one line, Jaidev the old poet, Bhikhan's medicine. And now the Bhatts, who brought their trade of praise to the Gurus and used it to point at the light.
screen: `SWAYYE: VERSES OF PRAISE, GURU BY GURU.` · `ONE LIGHT, LAMP FROM LAMP.` · `NOT THE PERSON: WHAT PASSES BETWEEN.` · `A WEEK OF OTHER VOICES.` · then, large: `POETS OF PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose goodness you've seen up close: not their looks or success, but patience, honesty, a kindness nobody noticed. Like a Bhatt, be specific: find the exact moment you saw it, then look for what's underneath, the light in them that isn't only theirs. If you pray, breathe out Waheguru.
Bhatt. A bard, a poet of praise. In the Granth, the Bhatts' swayye praise the Gurus as one light passed from Guru to Guru.
Your line: poets of praise. Good praise is specific, and it can point past the person. Day seven hundred ninety-one, done.
